# Mūgapakkhajātaka (Ja 538)

**ID:** Ja 538
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538), commonly known across Southeast Asia as the *Temiya-jātaka*, is the first narrative of the *Mahānipāta* or "Ten Great Jātakas" [Wood 2005; Appleton 2010; Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities]. Set at Jetavana, the Buddha introduces the story to illustrate that even prior to perfecting his wisdom, he had relinquished royal power to renounce the world. In this past life, the Bodhisatta is born as Prince Temiya (Mūgapakkhapaṇḍita), the son of the king of Kāsi [Fausböll 1897; Appleton 2010]. Observing his father punishing criminals and reflecting that wielding state power inevitably brings bad kamma leading to hell, Temiya feigns being deaf, mute, and crippled to escape kingship [Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities; Appleton 2010; Lele, Disengaged Buddhism]. Eventually conveyed to the forest to be killed and buried, he reveals his strength to the charioteer digging his grave and renounces worldly life, inspiring his parents and royal court to adopt ascetic seclusion [Wood 2005; Appleton 2010]. In the Theravāda tradition, the story exemplifies the Bodhisatta's perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) [Appleton 2010; Crosby 2014].

 DharmaNexus confirms substantial text reuse with the *Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 134, §121.1–121.4), other *Jātakas* such as the *Soṇanandajātaka* (Ja 532), *Vidhurajātaka* (Ja 546), and *Vessantarajātaka* (Ja 547), and the *Cariyāpiṭaka* (Cp 26) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages with Tibetan Vinaya texts, the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā*, and Chinese Āgamas (T 26, T 99, T 100), and scholarship notes a Tocharian version [DharmaNexus; Skilling and Saerji, How the Buddhas]. The jātaka appears in early epigraphy and art on an inscribed medallion at the Bharhut stūpa (*Mugaphakaya Jātaka*) [Wood 2005; Cunningham 1879] and continues to serve as an inspirational exemplar for modern Theravāda forest monks [Crosby 2014].
